AGENCY DKT. NO. PFRS #80736
BETTY REED,
Petitioner,
v.
POLICE AND FIREMEN'S RETIREMENT
SYSTEM,

Frank M. Crivelli, Esq., for petitioner (Pellettieri, Rabstein & Altman, attorneys)
Danielle P. Bradus, Deputy Attorney General, for respondent (Ann Milgram, Attorney General of New Jersey, attorney
Record Closed: June 8, 2009 Decided: October 23, 2009
BEFORE JOSEPH F. MARTONE, ALJ:
STATEMENT OF THE CASE AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY
Petitioner, Betty Reed, who was employed by the Department of Corrections as a Senior Correction Officer at the New
Jersey State Prison, seeks an accidental disability retirement, alleging an incident that occurred on December 16, 2006, was a
traumatic event. The Board of Trustees of the Police and Firemen's Retirement System (PFRS) found that Ms. Reed was not totally
and permanently disabled from the performance of her regular and assigned job duties, that the incident was not a traumatic event,
and the alleged disability was not a direct result of the incident because the event was not undesigned and unexpected. Ms. Reed
requested a hearing, and the matter was transmitted to the Office of Administrative Law (OAL) on March 4, 2008, for hearing as a
contested case.
The matter was assigned to me on April 1, 2008, and a hearing was scheduled for and held on January 14, 2009. The record remained
open at the conclusion of the hearing and was closed on June 8, 2009, after the submission of written closing arguments. As a result
of orders of extension, the time for filing the initial decision was extended until October 23, 2009.
FACTUAL DISCUSSION
Stipulated facts
The parties to this case entered into a Joint Stipulation of Facts. (J-1.) I have summarized the stipulated facts in the paragraphs which
follow.
Petitioner, Betty Reed, was born on November 11, 1963. (J​-2.) She began work for the New Jersey State Prison as a Correction Officer
Recruit on August 31, 1996. (J-2.) Petitioner was injured on December 16, 2006 opening the brake on the flat tier. (J-3.)
On or about July 10, 2007, petitioner filed an application for an accidental disability retirement with an effective date of January 1, 2008.
(J-4.) At the time petitioner filed her application for accidental disability retirement she was employed as a Senior Correction Officer. (J-4 and J-
5.)
On December 10, 2007, the Board of Trustees, Police and Firemen's Retirement System (PFRS Board) determined that petitioner was
not totally and permanently disabled from the performance of her regular and assigned job duties. Further, the Board determined that the incident

of December 16, 2006, was not considered a traumatic event, and the alleged disability was not a direct result of the incident as detailed by
N.J.S.A. 43:16A-7 and relevant case law. Finally, the Board determined that the event was not undesigned and unexpected. (J-6.)
On January 24, 2008, petitioner's attorney, Frank M. Crivelli, Esq., appealed the December 10, 2007, determination of the PFRS Board
and requested an administrative hearing. (J-7.) On February 11, 2008 the PFRS Board approved the petitioner's request for a hearing and the
matter was transmitted to the Office of Administrative Law (OAL) for hearing as a contested case. (J-8.)
Each of the joint exhibits referred to above was admitted into evidence without the necessity of formal proof or authentication based upon
the stipulation of the parties. Of particular interest are the petitioner's Application for Disability Retirement of August 2007, (J-4), wherein the
petitioner describes the incident in question and the Senior Correction Officer Job Description, (J-5.) In addition, petitioner's entire pension file, P-
1, was accepted in evidence without objection.
Hearing testimony
This summary sets forth portions of the testimony relating to those facts which I found to be relevant to the issues before me.
Testimony of Betty Reed
Petitioner was employed as a senior correction officer at the New Jersey State Prison. She had been a correction officer for eleven years.
Petitioner briefly described the responsibilities of a correction officer as "to go home safe, for other correction officers to go home safe and for the
inmates not to go home." Her daily duties were to maintain order and control of the institution. This included controlling the flow of inmate traffic to
and from the mess hall and other daily activities; to maintain control; to prevent incidents involving inmates with each other and with correction
officers; to make sure there were no disturbances; and to maintain control during standing movements. While the inmates were in the mess hall it
was her duty to watch the inmates and to keep them in control.
Petitioner's daily uniform included a bullet-proof jacket and, when she was in the presence of inmates, also included a helmet, a vest and a
baton. When there was a disturbance a correction officer was required to obtain and dress in riot gear.
Petitioner testified that she was injured on December 16, 2006. At the time she was working in Unit 2 Right, which is in the old section of
the prison. There were approximately 132 inmates in that unit. In the morning her first duty was to awaken each of the inmates while in their cell,
count the inmates, and log where they were going. If the inmates were scheduled to be somewhere their cell would have to be opened. Each cell is
double-locked and there is a two-step process to releasing the inmate for movement elsewhere. The first step is to unlock the individual cell doors
of those inmates who were to leave their cells. At that point all of the cell doors remained locked by a "bar brake" and it was Ms. Reed's duty to
unlock and open the bar brake in order to release the cell doors that had been previously unlocked.
Petitioner described the bar brake as being 60 to 75 feet long. She had to remove a large padlock from the bar brake and pull the bar
brake to allow the individual doors to open. She explained that the doors are 100-150 years old and because of loss of maintenance personnel,
the doors and bar brake have not been lubricated in quite some time. It was necessary for her to exert a great deal of effort in pulling the bar brake
and she hurt herself in doing this. When she did so on December 16, 2006, she immediately felt pain that felt like a "crick" in her neck. As time
went on during that day, the pain in her neck got worse and worse and traveled to the middle of her back and then to her lower back until
eventually it involved her entire back, hips and legs. Even the bottom of her feet felt like they were burning.
Petitioner was unable to finish her duty on December 16, 2006. She remained long enough to walk the tiers and do the count with the
replacement correction officer. She explained she did not want to be a "code 21" which would require all of the prisoners to be counted.
Petitioner was sent to Robert Wood Johnson Hospital for treatment. They took an X-ray and gave her an injection for the pain. The next
day she went to Corporate Health Center where she was seen by Virginia Gaskel, D.O. Dr. Gaskel treated her for approximately one-and-a-half
months. During that time she was sent to Novacare for physical therapy. She had an MRI and was then discharged by Dr. Gaskel and sent to
Trenton Orthopedics where she was seen by Marc J. Levine, M.D., until May 2007. Dr. Levine treated her but eventually came to the conclusion
that physical therapy at Novacare was making her condition worse. Dr. Levine then sent her to Dr. Feder, a pain management specialist who
injected her with four cortisone shots and one botox shot to relieve her pain. These shots were injected approximately every ten days. The shots
helped relieve her pain a great deal, but the pain kept coming back. In the meantime, workers' compensation had discharged her.
Because the pain increased she was sent back to Dr. Levine who said he could not do anything further to help her. He then sent her back
to Dr. Feder who said she was at her maximum improvement and he could not do anything further. Dr. Feder gave her prescriptions for Flexeril
and Napersan. Dr. Levine then sent her for a functional capacity evaluation by Kinematic Consultants in May 2007. She explained that the
evaluation involved various kinds of activities such as running and kneeling, some of which she was unable to perform.
The results of the functional capacity evaluation were given to Dr. Levine and he told her that she failed the evaluation. Based on the
evaluation she was placed on permanent restrictions on her employment for light duty only and could not return to work as a correction officer. Dr.
Levine discharged her by telling her that there was no treatment for her. All of the doctors who had treated her, including Dr. Levine, had been

chosen by her employer.
Petitioner then received a letter from the Department of Corrections dated June 18, 2007 (P-1(L)), explaining that because of Dr. Levine's
opinion, she could not return to work, and requesting that she meet with the Division of Pensions to discuss her retirement options. The letter said
that her noncompliance with the request would require the Department to process an involuntary retirement on her behalf. The PBA, her collective
bargaining unit, advised her to fill out the paperwork for a disability retirement, which she did. She was required to obtain certificates from two
physicians that she could not return to work. She was only able to obtain a certificate from Dr. Levine stating that she could return to light category
work but could not return to her regular, full-time duties. Dr. Gaskel could not complete the certificate because the petitioner had been discharged
by her for orthopedic treatment. The Division of Pensions then sent her to a doctor and she eventually received a letter denying her pension. She
then began the appeal process.
Petitioner testified that she was a correction officer for almost eleven years and would love to return to work, but she does not feel she is
capable of doing so. She would not be able to qualify for firearms because she could not shoot a pistol let alone a shotgun because of her injury
and pain. She would not be able to put on a helmet or vest. She would not be able to stand up for two hours during inmate movements. More than
anything else she feels she cannot respond to back up a fellow correction officer if there is trouble with an inmate. She cannot even zip up her
dress. She cannot get her hair done because she cannot hold her head in a chair to have it washed. If she goes shopping she is unable to lift or
carry a case of water. She cannot wash her back and her daughter must wash her. She would be unable to take off her boots. She has a terrible
problem sleeping and cannot lay on her stomach and sleep. If she moves in her sleep the pain wakes her up and then keeps her awake.
Upon my questioning the petitioner explained that before the injury, she was in good shape and could do pull ups, sit ups, and push ups.
Because of the pain she experiences in everyday activities she is unable to run or exercise. If she is required to dress in riot gear as part of her
duties, the weight of the helmet, the vest, and other riot gear would cause her to be in severe pain. She explained that if there is a code 33, where
another correction officer is in trouble, all other officers must respond and if they are not able to they should be fired. She would be unable to
respond and would be unable to help her fellow correction officers. She restated that her biggest concern would be backing up a fellow correction
officer who is in trouble.
Petitioner was earning $72,000 a year as a correction officer. Her last full pay was in May 2007, and her last check for accrued leave was
in December 2007. She has exhausted all of her savings and has no money for anything. She would have obtained a physician to testify in this
matter but had no funds in order to do so.
With regard to previous injuries, petitioner testified that in June 2001 she was hit by an ambulance and her lower back was bruised and
treated. She is fully recovered from this injury. Petitioner also had a right shoulder injury in connection with the firing of a shotgun in approximately
2004 and had rotator cuff surgery. She recovered from this and was able to return to work. She has not received treatment for any other injury
between 2001 and 2006. She does not recall seeing the independent medical examiner for the Division of Pensions. She admitted that she locked
and unlocked the cells every day prior to the injury and she used the same amount of force each day. Her actions on the day of the injury were the
same as she always did previously.
Ms. Reed testified that she knows she cannot do the job of a correction officer. She cannot backup a partner if needed but would be able
to push a button. She explained that one of the partners would be in the booth pushing the buttons, but the other partner would be in a suit and
helmet doing movements. She could not stand and do movements for that long. Any rotation of assignments is based on the directions of the
supervisor and on seniority. She is not currently seeing a doctor other than her primary doctor who gives her prescriptions to deal with her
continuing pain.
Testimony of Lawrence I. Barr, D.O.
Dr. Lawrence I. Barr, respondent's independent medical expert, testified to his educational background and his extensive training and experience
as an orthopedic surgeon. He was accepted as an expert witness in orthopedics.
Dr. Barr examined the petitioner on October 5, 2007, in order to determine whether she was disabled from her job as a correction officer. (R-2.)
He reviewed petitioner's job specification but could not recall if he did so at the time of the examination or at some later date. He took a history
from the petitioner and then performed a physical examination consisting of range of motion testing. He found that the petitioner had normal range
of motion in her neck, shoulders, elbows and wrists. He also found normal ranges of motion in her lower back, although he did find tenderness in
petitioner's neck. He reviewed the medical records provided to him and as a result of his review of these records and his objective examination of
petitioner's range of motion he found that petitioner was not totally and permanently disabled from her job as a corrections officer.
Dr. Barr also testified concerning his consideration of a functional capacity evaluation that was conducted on petitioner. He explained that such an
evaluation is a snapshot in time and provides recommendations for a treating doctor. He does not use such evaluations in his practice. While
petitioner's evaluation appeared to be a valid test, he indicated there was no correlation to his findings on his physical examination. He explained
that the normal progression of a neck sprain is to improve.

In his report Dr. Barr stated that if the entire decision was based solely on the functional capacity evaluation, petitioner would be totally and
permanently disabled from her regular assigned duties. However, based on his total assessment of petitioner, he did not reach the same conclusion
as either of petitioner's treating physicians.
On cross-examination, Dr. Barr admitted that an MRI report of petitioner's cervical spine revealed a bulging disc at the C3-4 level. He admitted
that a bulging disc in the cervical spine does have the potential to cause radicular symptoms in the upper extremities and shoulder area. In addition
to tingling and numbness, other symptoms would include loss of mobility and strength, which are the same symptoms as those stated by the
petitioner.
LEGAL DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS
This proceeding arises as a result of petitioner's application for an accidental disability retirement and respondent's denial of
that application. The statutory authority for the grant of an accidental disability retirement to a public employee enrolled in the Police
and Firemen's Retirement System is found at N.J.S.A. 43:16A-7. This provides in relevant part:
(1) Upon the written application by a member in service, by one acting in his behalf or by his employer any member
may be retired on an accidental disability retirement allowance; provided, that the medical board, after a medical
examination of such member, shall certify that the member is permanently and totally disabled as a direct result of a
traumatic event occurring during and as a result of the performance of his regular or assigned duties and that such
disability was not the result of the member's willful negligence and that such member is mentally or physically
incapacitated for the performance of his usual duty and of any other available duty in the department which his
employer is willing to assign to him.
The critical fact which must be established in order to entitle a public employee to an accidental disability retirement pension is that the
disability was caused by a "traumatic event." Thus, the issue in this matter is whether the incident as described by the rose to the level of a
"traumatic event" as that term has been defined by case law?
The petitioner has the burden of proving all of the elements necessary to show eligibility for an accidental disability retirement allowance.
This must be shown by a fair preponderance of the legally competent evidence. In re Polk License Revocation, 90 N.J. 550, 560 (1982);
Atkinson v. Parsekian, 37 N.J. 143, 149 (1962).
The Supreme Court in Richardson v. Board of Trustees, Police and Firemen's Retirement System, 192 N.J. 189, 212-213 (2007) has set
forth the test necessary to meet the statutory requirement. It states that to obtain accidental disability benefits, a member must prove:
1. that he [or she] is permanently and totally disabled;
2. as a direct result of a traumatic event that is
a. identifiable as to time and place,
b. undesigned and unexpected, and
c. caused by a circumstance external to the member (not the result of pre-existing disease that is aggravated or accelerated by the
work);
3. that the traumatic event occurred during and as a result of the member's regular or assigned duties;
4. that the disability was not the result of the member's willful negligence; and
5. that the member is mentally or physically incapacitated from performing his usual or any other duty.
Undisputed issues.
Because there is no dispute in this case as to certain of the requirements of Richardson, I am briefly addressing them.
In his report dated October 5, 2007 (R-2), Dr. Barr states:
I find causal relationship between the work injury of December 16, 2006 and the cervical sprain, shoulder
strain and right low back sprain. These were reported in a timely fashion. The mechanism stated is
consistent with the injuries suffered. She did have a prior injury to her low back in 2001, but those
symptoms resolved. My opinion is held within a reasonable degree of medical probability.
Based on the quoted language I FIND that the petitioner's injuries were the direct result of the incident of December 16, 2006. The
question whether this incident was a traumatic event is addressed below.
Based on the petitioner's undisputed testimony concerning the incident of December 16, 2006, I FIND that the incident in question
occurred during and as a result of the member's regular or assigned duties, and that the petitioner's disability was not the result of the member's
willful negligence. Therefore, parts three and four of the Richardson test appear to be met. Part five of Richardson involving whether the member is
physically incapacitated from performing his usual or any other duty is included and addressed in the discussion whether the petitioner is
permanently and totally disabled.

Therefore, the issues remaining to be decided are whether the petitioner is permanently and totally disabled as required by part 1 of
Richardson, and whether the traumatic event requirements of part two through five of Richardson have been satisfied.
Is the petitioner permanently and totally disabled?
In determining whether petitioner is permanently and totally disabled, the test to be applied is whether or not the applicant is employable in
the general area of his or her ordinary employment. Getty v. Prison Officers' Pension Fund, 85 N.J. Super. 383 (App. Div. 1964); Skulski v.
Nolan, 68 N.J. 179 (1975). Whether an individual is physically incapacitated or disabled in the general area of his or her ordinary employment is a
fact question that involves medical proofs and special expertise. See, Katz v. Township of Howell, 67 N.J. 51, 62-63 (1975). An exception to this
are disabilities which are apparent to laymen. Lesniak v. County of Bergen, 117 N.J. 12, 31-32 (1989).
The proofs in support of the petitioner's position consist primarily of her own undisputed testimony and her statements to examining and
treating physicians with respect to her physical complaints and disability. She stated that her pain started at work on December 16, 2006, when it
was necessary for her to exert a great deal of effort pulling a bar brake to allow cell doors to open. In exerting this effort she suffered an injury she
described as starting with a "crick" in her neck, but became increasingly painful and traveled to her back, lower back and even into her hips and
legs as the day went on. She was unable to finish work on that day and had to seek treatment for the pain. The pain has persisted despite her being
treated with prescriptions for pain medications and muscle relaxants, cortisone and botox injections and physical therapy.. Because of the pain, she
has difficulty sleeping, standing, walking, and with daily activities such as bathing, dressing, cooking, and housework. She is also unable to exercise.
She is seriously concerned about her ability to qualify for firearms, dress in riot gear, restrain prisoners or back up other correction officers in
trouble. I FIND petitioner's testimony to be credible with respect to her physical complaints.
Petitioner's testimony as to the extent of her pain and disability is supported by the reports and actions of Dr. Levine, the physician who
was authorized by petitioner's employer to treat her. After concluding that there was no further treatment for petitioner, Dr. Levine discharged her
after he placed her on permanent restrictions on her employment for light duty only. This meant that she could not return to work as a correction
officer. As a result of this, the Department of Corrections sent petitioner a letter on June 18, 2007, (P-1L), stating that because of Dr. Levine's
opinion, petitioner could not return to work and she should take steps to retire. In connection with her retirement application, the petitioner
obtained a certificate from Dr. Levine stating that she was unable to return to her regular, full-time duties. (P-1V2.)
Petitioner's testimony is somewhat supported by the testimony and report of Dr. Barr. In his report of October 5, 2007, (R-2), Dr. Barr
reviewed the functional capacity evaluation of May 2007, and stated he felt that the evaluation is compatible with mild residual functional movement
issues and moderate residual functional strength issues. He went on to say it appeared that this evaluation was a valid test and demonstrated that
petitioner had the ability to engage in light category work.
Also supportive of the petitioner's position was Dr. Barr's acknowledgement on cross-examination that an MRI of petitioner showed a
bulging disc at the C3-4 level in petitioner's cervical spine, which had the potential to cause symptoms in petitioner's upper extremities and shoulder
areas. He admitted the symptoms would include tingling, numbness, loss of mobility and strength, and these are the same symptoms as those stated
by the petitioner.
Most damaging to the petitioner's claim of permanent and total disability was Dr. Barr's testimony at the hearing and his report as to his
physical examination of the petitioner. In testimony, Dr. Barr acknowledged that if the decision was based on the functional capacity evaluation,
petitioner would be totally and permanently disabled. He explained that the functional capacity evaluation is a "snapshot" and its purpose is to
provide recommendations to the treating doctor. However, based on the lack of objective findings in his clinical evaluation of the petitioner, he
overruled the functional capacity evaluation.
Dr. Barr's orthopedic examination showed that petitioner had a full range of motion of her shoulders, elbows and wrists. She had good
strength, reflexes and sensation. This led to his diagnosis of a cervical sprain, shoulder strain and right low back sprain. Even though the MRI
showed a bulging disc at C3-4 which could explain petitioner's claimed symptoms, because petitioner had full range of motion and good strength,
reflexes and sensation when he examined her, it was Dr. Barr's opinion that petitioner is not totally and permanently disabled from the performance
of her assigned job duties as a correction officer.
Attorney for petitioner argues that I should find the petitioner permanently and totally disabled based on her testimony as to her disability
supported by the reports and the opinion expressed by Dr. Levine as her authorized treating physician that she is permanently and totally disabled.
This opinion appears to be supported by the functional capacity evaluation and the MRI showing a bulging disc at C3-4.
However, I feel constrained to accept the opinion expressed by Dr. Barr in his testimony, even though it appears to differ from his own
report, because his is the only opinion that was elicited at the hearing under oath. Also, in fairness to Dr. Barr, his opinion is based primarily on his
orthopedic examination which showed that petitioner had a full range of motion of her shoulders, elbows and wrists. I cannot disregard the results
of this examination and base my decision on Dr. Levine's opinion since it is hearsay evidence and cannot be relied upon to establish an ultimate
finding of fact. N.J.A.C. 1:1-15.5(b).

It is troubling to me is that the petitioner has been prevented from returning to work by the opinion expressed by Dr. Levine as her
authorized treating physician that she is permanently and totally disabled. It would be even more troubling if the petitioner is not reinstated as a
correction officer because of Dr. Levine's certification that she is permanently and totally disabled when she is being denied an accidental disability
pension because she is not permanently and totally disabled. The unfairness of such a situation cries out for a remedy.
Notwithstanding the above, I must make findings based on the record before me. Based on Dr. Barr's testimony at the hearing, and
because of the absence in the record of this case of legally competent evidence to the contrary, I FIND that the petitioner is not permanently and
totally disabled and she is employable in the general area of her ordinary employment.
Was the incident described by the petitioner a traumatic event?
Petitioner's undisputed testimony with respect to the incident of December 16, 2006, was credible. Her testimony is that it was necessary
for her to exert a great deal of effort pulling the bar break to allow cell doors to open. In exerting this effort she felt pain in her neck which traveled
to her back and lower back.
The first question is whether the traumatic event requirements of part two and three have been satisfied. The Richardson Court defines
traumatic event essentially in the same way that it has historically understood an accident to be "-an unexpected external happening that directly
causes injury and is not the result of pre-existing disease alone or in combination with work effort." Ibid.
Less clear is whether the event in question was undesigned and unexpected as a matter of law. In defining traumatic event in the same way
as an accident is defined, the Richardson Court noted that the "undesigned and unexpected" part of the test comes from a line of workers'
compensation cases defining "accident" as "an unlooked for mishap or untoward event which is not expected or designed." Id. at 197. See,
Williams v. Port Auth. of N.Y. & N.J., 175 N.J. 82, 88 (2003); Ciuba v. Irvington Varnish & Insulator Co., 27 N.J. 127, 134 (1958); Spindler v.
Universal Chain Corp., 11 N.J. 34, 38 (1952); Bollinger v. Wagaraw Bldg. Supply Co., 122 N.J.L. 512, 519 (E. & A. 1939); Bryant v. Fissell,
84 N.J.L. 72, 76 (Sup. Ct. 1913). The Richardson Court provides some guidance as to the terms "undesigned and unexpected" with its reference
to its earlier decision in Russo v. Teachers' Pension and Annuity Fund, 62 N.J. 142 (1973). There, the definition of an accident was not limited to
just unintended external events. Chief Justice Weintraub, drawing from a line of insurance policy interpretation cases to analyze the concept of
accidental injury in an accidental death benefit case stated:
In those cases, we concluded that when an insurance policy does not purport to cover an unexpected injury as
such, there must be something about the preceding acts and events, alone or in the light of the unexpected injurious
result, to lead an ordinary person to call the means "accidental," even though, strictly speaking, nothing unexpected
or unforeseen occurred in the course of the preceding acts. [citation omitted]. In ordinary parlance, an accident
may be found either in an unintended external event or in an unanticipated consequence of an intended external
event if that consequence is extraordinary or unusual in common experience. Injury by ordinary work effort or
strain to a diseased heart, although unexpected by the individual afflicted, is not an extraordinary or unusual
consequence in common experience. We are satisfied that disability or death in such circumstances is not
accidental within the meaning of a pension statute when all that appears is that the employee was doing his usual
work in the usual way. [emphasis supplied]
[Russo, at 154].
Consistent with the Russo analysis, strictly speaking, nothing unexpected or unforeseen occurred regarding Ms. Reed's activities which
preceded her injury. I FIND, however, that petitioner's injury was an unanticipated consequence of her intended actions, which consequence is
extraordinary or unusual in common experience. As such, she satisfies the "undesigned and unexpected" element of the Richardson test. This is so
despite the fact that petitioner's job responsibilities includes the expectation that a correction officer has the strength and ability to open a bar brake
to release inmates from their cells.
It may be claimed that the event was not external to Ms. Reed but that the injury was the result of her own work effort of exerting force
while opening the bar brake. The Richardson Court abandoned the prior requirement of Kane v. Board of Trustees, Police and Firemen's
Retirement System, etc., 100 N.J. 651, 663 (1985), that the member be a victim of a great rush of force or power that he himself did not bring
into motion. It instead simplified the inquiry to whether the injury was caused by a circumstance external to the member with a rush of force being
but one example of an external circumstance. Indeed, the event began with Reed's own work effort while exerting pressure on the bar brake. The
resistance of the bar brake is no less a circumstance external to Ms. Reed simply because it represented an immovable object as opposed to an
active force. What is required is a force or cause external to the worker. Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 211.
The Richardson Court's recitation of the purpose behind the amending statute in 1964 for Accidental Retirement disability benefits is
instructive.
. . . In amending the statute, the Legislature sought to prohibit the grant of accidental disability benefits to a member
disabled by a pre-existing condition, alone or in combination with work effort, no more and no less. . . .
Therefore, when our cases have observed that the amendments were intended to make obtaining accidental
disability benefits "more difficult" they were correct but incomplete. The real question is: "more difficult than what?"
The answer is: more difficult than the broad workers' compensation causation standard that included heart attacks
suffered at work by members with pre-existing heart disease. Only the pre-existing condition category of qualifying

events was at issue during the amendatory process. [citations omitted].
[Richardson, supra,192 N.J. at 210]
The Court emphasizes, with the parenthetical reference following its "circumstance external" element of the traumatic event test, the specific
limitation the Legislature sought to impose on the grant of an Accidental Retirement disability benefit—"not the result of pre-existing disease that is
aggravated or accelerated by the work."
The injury suffered by the petitioner caused by the event in question does not fall into the category which the Legislature intended to
exclude from coverage by the Accidental Disability retirement statute as something other than caused by a circumstance external to the member.
Petitioner's injury was "not the result of pre-existing disease that is aggravated or accelerated by the work." While there is some evidence in the
record that petitioner had suffered prior injuries, there is no evidence in the record and no suggestion by respondent's medical expert that the injury
here was the result of preexisting disease alone or in combination with work effort. She suffered a bruised lower back in 2001 for which she was
treated, and she suffered a rotator cuff injury in 2004 which was repaired by surgery. Otherwise she received no treatment for any other injury
between 2001 and 2006.
Upon consideration of all of the surrounding circumstances, I FIND the consequence of Ms. Reed's acts was extraordinary and unusual in
common experience, unlike that of a diseased heart. See, Russo v. Teachers' Pension and Annuity Fund, supra at 154. I additionally FIND that a
circumstance external to Reed caused her injury. I CONCLUDE that this satisfies the requirements of part two of the Richardson Court's test for
a traumatic event.
Conclusion
I have found that the petitioner has failed to meet the requirement of Richardson that she is permanently and totally disabled. Because the
petitioner has failed to meet all of the requirements to qualify for Accidental Disability retirement benefits, I CONCLUDE that her application
should be DENIED.
DECISION AND ORDER
For the reasons stated above, I ORDER that petitioner's application for an accidental disability retirement is DENIED.
I hereby FILE my initial decision with the BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF THE POLICE AND FIREMEN'S RETIREMENT SYSTEM for
consideration.
This recommended decision may be adopted, modified or rejected by the BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF THE POLICE AND FIREMEN'S
RETIREMENT SYSTEM, which by law is authorized to make a final decision in this matter. If the Board of Trustees of the Police and

this recommended decision shall become a final decision in accordance with N.J.S.A. 52:14B-10.
